design_detail: Short critical history (accepted manuscript of an article in a journal series that also revisited Robins's Vietnam studies, ref. 1) of the three 'Rat Park' experiments run by Bruce Alexander and colleagues at Simon Fraser University: Alexander, Coambs & Hadaway (1978), Hadaway et al. (1979) and Alexander et al. (1981). It describes the enclosure and the measurement methods, tabulates each study's group sizes, procedures and main findings (Table 1), lists design and reporting limitations, summarizes three independent housing studies (Hill & Powell 1976; Bozarth et al., dated 1987 in the text and 1989 in the reference list; Petrie 1996), and discusses how the popular account came to differ from the papers. No search strategy, no inclusion criteria, no formal appraisal and no new data. Every experimental finding it summarizes is in rats.
can_establish: What the three original Rat Park papers reported according to two independent readers (group sizes, measurement methods, the specific conditions under which housing differences appeared, the original authors' cautious conclusions), and how far the popular account has moved from those papers.
cannot_establish: Whether housing changes drug intake in rats in general, or anything about environment and addiction in people (no new data; the human arguments are cited, not tested); its summaries of the original papers and of the replication attempts are second-hand, and one of them (Petrie 1996, read for this round) is attributed to the wrong original study.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (narrative review). The Rat Park studies as tabulated (Table 1, PDF pp. 8–10): 1978, 32 albino Wistar rats (isolated 4 females and 6 males; Rat Park 10 females and 12 males), 27 remaining after deaths; 1979, 36 rats (9 females and 9 males per housing condition); 1981, 32 rats in four groups of 4 females and 4 males (isolated throughout, Rat Park throughout, and the two groups switched at 65 days).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: No criteria stated; the studies discussed were chosen by the authors.
sample.attrition: Not applicable to the review. For the 1978 study the text reports four deaths, but its own group counts (32 to 27 rats) and Table 1 give five (see reporting issues).
sample.selection_effects: Selection is the authors' own. The replication section names three studies with results in both directions; later animal work on enrichment and drug seeking is mentioned in one sentence without citations to specific drug studies, and choice studies offering rats a non-drug alternative are not discussed. Neither author is an author of the Rat Park papers (refs. 16–18).

exposure.measurement: Not applicable as a review. As summarized: oral morphine hydrochloride solution (with or without sucrose) offered beside water; isolated rats' bottles were weighed and corrected against a bottle on an empty cage, while Rat Park rats drank from a dispenser that released single drops, counted and filmed together with the drinking rat's identifying mark (PDF p. 2, The original 1978 study, 2nd paragraph).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions in rats, as tabulated (Table 1, PDF pp. 8–10). 1978: housing from weaning; a limited-access period (fluid 7 h a day on a 3-day cycle, 9 cycles); 57 days with morphine solution as the only fluid (4 choice days); Nichols cycles (8 three-day cycles, 4 choice days); an abstinence period with choice days after 2 and 5 weeks. 1979: morphine-naive rats offered tap water against 0.5 mg/ml morphine hydrochloride with sucrose rising from 0 to 10%, then 0.3 and 0.15 mg/ml in 10% sucrose, 5 days per solution. 1981: a quinine bitter-sweet control, then 1, 0.5, 0.3 and 0.15 mg/ml morphine hydrochloride in 10% sucrose, 5 days per solution.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable; the 1978 study included an abstinence period with choice tests after 2 and 5 weeks without morphine (Table 1, PDF p. 8).

comparison.controls: Within the original studies: rats housed alone in 18 × 25 × 18 cm cages without sight of other rats, against the mixed-sex Rat Park colony in an L-shaped 8.8 m² enclosure with sawdust, open boxes, tubes, open-topped cages and a climbing pole (PDF p. 2).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable to the review; how rats were allocated to housing in the original studies is not described.

outcomes.instruments: As summarized: morphine solution and water intake per rat on choice days and in forced-access periods, with sex and housing effects tested by F tests (Table 1, PDF pp. 8–10).
outcomes.validity_norms: The review's central measurement criticism: intake was measured by different methods in the two housing conditions, so a systematic error in one (for example unrecorded leakage from the isolated cages' bottles) could create a group difference; the authors note that water intake did not show the same pattern, which offers some protection (PDF p. 3, Follow-up studies, 3rd paragraph).
outcomes.operationalization: The original studies measured oral morphine intake; the review treats this as one behaviour under one manipulation (housing), not as a model of addiction (PDF p. 4, Legacy, 2nd paragraph).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable to the review; the authors say the original studies made many comparisons in very small groups, raising the risk of false-positive results (PDF p. 3, Follow-up studies, 3rd paragraph; PDF p. 5, Conclusion, 1st paragraph).

analysis.effect_sizes: As cited from the original studies (Table 1, PDF pp. 8–10). 1978: limited-access data not presented because of measurement error; forced-access period, mean intake higher in Rat Park rats (18.6 mg morphine hydrochloride per rat) than in isolated rats (13.3 mg); Nichols cycles, isolated rats drank less on non-choice days but more on choice days (F=200.9, df 1/69, p<0.001); abstinence period, isolated rats drank more (F 26.38, df 1/23, p<0.001); females drank more than males (F 7.26, df 1/23, p<0.05; F=67.86, df 1/69, p<0.001; F=36.44, df 1/23, p<0.001). 1979: little evidence of a housing effect at high morphine and low sucrose; with 10% sucrose isolated rats drank more morphine solution, the largest difference at 0.15 mg/ml; sex differences inconsistent. 1981: rats living in Rat Park at testing drank less morphine solution than isolated rats regardless of early housing (F=33.64, p<0.0001, df not printed); no early-housing effect; weak evidence of an interaction; differences driven mainly by males. Amounts consumed are given only for the 1978 forced-access period.
analysis.selective_reporting: Not applicable as a review. The table gives F tests and directions but, apart from the 1978 forced-access means, no amounts consumed, so the size of the housing effects cannot be judged from this source.
analysis.power: Not applicable; the authors call the group sizes very small even for an animal study (PDF p. 2, The original 1978 study, 3rd paragraph).

interpretation_gap.results_show: Three small rat experiments from one laboratory, with intake measured differently in the two housing conditions, found less oral morphine intake in colony-housed than in isolated rats under particular conditions (choice days after forced exposure, sweetened low-concentration solutions, housing at the time of testing), while Rat Park rats consumed more than isolated rats during forced access. The original authors drew cautious conclusions and did not link the findings to human addiction; independent housing studies gave mixed results.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The unlabelled summary paragraph at the head of the article (PDF p. 1) states the housing effect without qualification (enriched rats drank less whether pre-exposed, naive, or raised in either housing). The body qualifies it: in 1979 differences appeared only at high sweetness and low morphine (PDF p. 3), and overall only in very specific conditions (PDF p. 5); Table 1 shows the opposite direction during forced access. The authors' own conclusion, that the popular reading of Rat Park as a new understanding of addiction is overstated and that it models one manipulation on one behaviour (PDF p. 4), is argued from the literature, and they still call its core message (addiction is more than a biological response to a drug) hugely important (PDF p. 5). The replication section names the wrong original study for Petrie's attempt (see reporting issues).

timeline.event: Hill & Powell: rats reared in enriched or impoverished conditions did not differ in morphine intake; enriched rats drank more cocaine solution (as summarized, PDF p. 4).
Alexander, Coambs & Hadaway: the original Rat Park study, 32 rats (as summarized, PDF p. 2 and Table 1).
Hadaway, Alexander, Coambs & Beyerstein: morphine-naive rats offered sweetened morphine solutions (as summarized, PDF p. 3 and Table 1).
Alexander, Beyerstein, Hadaway & Coambs: housing at testing, not early housing, went with intake; half the rats switched at 65 days (as summarized, PDF p. 3 and Table 1).
Bozarth, Murray & Wise: isolated rats acquired intravenous cocaine self-administration, socially housed rats not consistently (as summarized; dated 1987 in the text, PDF p. 4).
Petrie: two experiments did not reproduce lower intake in colony rats; designed as a replication of the 1981 study (read for this round).

replication.where_it_stands: Rat Park rests on three small experiments from one laboratory (1978–1981); the one published direct replication attempt read for this round (Petrie 1996) did not reproduce the housing effect, and the other housing studies summarized here point both ways. The popular version (rats in a rich environment refuse morphine) is not what the papers reported: Rat Park rats did drink morphine. All of it concerns oral morphine drinking in rats.

funding.funder: No funding statement in the accepted manuscript.
funding.affiliations_note: Department of Psychological Sciences, University of Liverpool (Gage) and Public Health Institute, Liverpool John Moores University (Sumnall). Recorded as context, not as a reason to discount the review.

what_would_settle_it: A preregistered, adequately powered replication of colony versus isolated housing in rats of both sexes (housed so that pregnancies cannot occur), with the same automated individual intake measurement in both conditions, random allocation, blinded analysis and more than one strain or supplier; and, for people, longitudinal or natural-experiment studies of how housing, opportunity and social exclusion change the course of drug use.

domains.note: No search, dates or criteria; the original papers and the replication attempts were chosen by the authors.

The original Rat Park studies are appraised in specific terms (measurement method, mixed-sex housing, group sizes, multiple comparisons), but the replication studies are summarized without any appraisal, and one is attributed to the wrong original study.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: None of the experiments discussed is the authors' own.

The body keeps the account of the studies apart from the authors' views, but the summary paragraph states the housing effect more generally than the body and Table 1 support, and statements about later enrichment research are made without the evidence.

domains.domain: Balance of evidence on housing and drug intake in animals
domains.note: The weaknesses of the original studies and the failed replication are set out in detail; later animal evidence that supports an environmental effect is mentioned in one sentence without citations to drug studies, so that side is the less documented one.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No standard instrument applies to a narrative review (METHODS §5.3). This short history gives a specific, checkable account of what the Rat Park papers reported (Table 1), names concrete design problems, and its authors have no stake in the studies; but selection is unsystematic, its summaries of other studies are second-hand, one count is internally inconsistent and one replication is attributed to the wrong study. Cite it for the history of Rat Park, the design limits of the original experiments and the gap between the papers and the popular account, labelled as rat findings; cite Petrie 1996 directly for the replication; do not cite it for anything about environment and addiction in people.

key_findings.finding: The 1978 study used 32 albino Wistar rats: 4 females and 6 males housed alone in 18 × 25 × 18 cm cages without sight of other rats, and 10 females and 12 males in Rat Park, an L-shaped 8.8 m² enclosure with sawdust, open boxes, tubes, open-topped cages and a climbing pole. For three weeks before the experiment all rats had water and a morphine hydrochloride solution and drank almost only water, in both housing conditions.
key_findings.locator: The original 1978 study, 1st paragraph (p. 2); Table 1, 1978 study row, Number of rats column (p. 8)

key_findings.finding: Intake was measured differently in the two housing conditions: isolated rats' bottles were weighed and corrected against a bottle on an empty cage for leakage and evaporation; Rat Park rats drank single drops from a dispenser whose counter and the drinking rat's mark were filmed. The authors point out that an error affecting only one method could produce a group difference where none existed; that water intake did not show the same pattern offers some protection.
key_findings.locator: The original 1978 study, 2nd paragraph (p. 2); Follow-up studies, 3rd paragraph (p. 3)

key_findings.finding: 1978 study as summarized: at the end, 2 isolated females, 6 isolated males, 7 Rat Park females and 12 Rat Park males remained; the isolated females (two rats) drank the most morphine in all periods; broadly, isolated rats drank more morphine than Rat Park rats and females more than males; across the choice days of the three-day cycle, intake rose in isolated rats and fell in Rat Park rats; Rat Park rats did drink morphine, contrary to some popular accounts.
key_findings.note: The text says four deaths; its own counts and Table 1 give five (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: Table 1, 1978 study: limited-access data were not presented because of measurement error; in the forced-access period (morphine solution the only fluid for 57 days), Rat Park rats consumed more on average than isolated rats (18.6 vs 13.3 mg morphine hydrochloride per rat); in the Nichols-cycle period, isolated rats drank less on non-choice days and more on choice days (F=200.9, df 1/69, p<0.001); in the abstinence period isolated rats drank more (F 26.38, df 1/23, p<0.001). Females drank more than males in the final forced-period choice days (F 7.26, df 1/23, p<0.05), the Nichols cycles (F=67.86, df 1/69, p<0.001) and abstinence (F=36.44, df 1/23, p<0.001).
key_findings.locator: Table 1, 1978 study row (Main findings and Other findings columns)

key_findings.finding: The original authors' conclusions were cautious: sex and housing are important variables and theories ignoring them risk oversimplification. Nowhere in the three papers did they connect the findings to human addiction or to deprivation; after ending the animal work, Alexander used Rat Park to develop an adaptive model of drug use in lectures, writings and a popular book.
key_findings.locator: The original 1978 study, 4th paragraph (p. 2); Follow-up studies, 4th paragraph (pp. 3–4)

key_findings.finding: 1979 study (morphine-naive rats; 9 females and 9 males per housing condition): a choice between tap water and a morphine solution made sweeter and then weaker in 5-day steps; isolated rats drank more morphine solution than Rat Park rats only at high sweetness and low morphine concentration (with 10% sucrose; largest difference at 0.15 mg/ml), with little evidence of a housing effect at high morphine and low sucrose.
key_findings.locator: Follow-up studies, 1st paragraph (p. 3); Table 1, 1979 study row (p. 9)
key_findings.note: The text says females again drank more than males; Table 1 calls the 1979 sex differences inconsistent (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: 1981 study (four groups of 4 females and 4 males: isolated or Rat Park from weaning, half of each switched at 65 days): rats living in Rat Park at the time of testing drank less morphine solution than isolated rats whatever their early housing (F=33.64, p<0.0001); no evidence that early housing mattered and weak evidence of an interaction; the housing difference was driven mainly by males.
key_findings.locator: Follow-up studies, 2nd paragraph (p. 3); Table 1, 1981 study row (pp. 9–10)

key_findings.finding: Limitations named by the authors: different intake measurement in the two housing conditions; males and females housed together in Rat Park with no account in the papers of pregnancies or pups; competition and dominance in the colony; very small groups with complex designs and many possible analyses, raising the risk of false positives; and group differences that emerged only in specific conditions (rats pre-exposed to morphine, particular morphine and sucrose concentrations, certain stages of the experiments).

Independent attempts gave mixed results: Hill & Powell (ref. 12, dated 1976 in the reference list) found no difference in morphine intake by rearing and more cocaine-solution drinking by enriched rats; Bozarth and colleagues found that isolated rats quickly learned to self-administer intravenous cocaine while socially housed rats did not consistently; Petrie (1996), in two experiments with two colony measurement methods, found colony rats drinking about as much morphine solution as Rat Park's colony rats but isolated rats drinking much less than Rat Park's isolated rats, and pointed to a change in the Wistar stock.
key_findings.locator: Replication attempts and contemporaneous studies, 1st paragraph (p. 4); reference list, refs. 12, 25 and 26 (p. 6)
key_findings.note: Second-hand summaries. Petrie (1996), read for this round (sc_petrie_1996), states it replicated Alexander et al. (1981), not the 1979 study named here. Bozarth et al. is dated 1987 here and 1989 in the reference list.

key_findings.finding: The authors judge the popular reading overstated: Rat Park models one manipulation (housing) on one behaviour (oral morphine intake) and was not particularly novel in its time; supply, availability and opportunity are proximal determinants of human drug use, and environment in human research also means access to services and social exclusion; most rodent self-administration studies still house animals individually; the story endured because policy advocacy needs a simple narrative.

reporting_issues.issue: The text says the 1978 study had four deaths, but by the editors' count its own group sizes at the start and end (32 rats, then 2 + 6 + 7 + 12 = 27; isolated females 4 to 2, Rat Park females 10 to 7) imply five, and Table 1 lists five (two females in each housing condition during forced access, one Rat Park female during abstinence).
reporting_issues.consequence: Five fits the counts and the df of 1/23 in Table 1 (27 rats in a 2 × 2 design); cite five deaths, and note that the isolated-female group ended with two rats.

reporting_issues.issue: Petrie (1996) is said to have tried to replicate the 1979 study (ref. 17), but Petrie states in his General Discussion that his experiments were designed to replicate Alexander et al. (1981) (see sc_petrie_1996), and his procedure (a quinine bitter-sweet phase, then morphine falling from 1.0 mg/ml in 10% sucrose) matches the 1981 design in this paper's own Table 1 (quinine phase, then 1, 0.5, 0.3 and 0.15 mg/ml in 10% sucrose), not the 1979 design (no quinine phase; 0.5 mg/ml with sucrose rising from 0 to 10%, then 0.3 and 0.15 mg/ml).
reporting_issues.consequence: The statement that Petrie's isolated rats drank much less than those in Rat Park compares them with the 1981 isolated rats; claims should name the 1981 study.

reporting_issues.issue: The text says the 1979 study again showed females drinking more morphine than males, but Table 1 calls that study's sex differences inconsistent (females drank less at 0.5 mg/ml with 1% sucrose and more at 0.3 and 0.15 mg/ml with 10% sucrose).
reporting_issues.consequence: Sex differences across the Rat Park studies should be described as inconsistent: females more in 1978, mixed in 1979, none in 1981 according to the text.

reporting_issues.issue: The unlabelled summary paragraph at the head of the article says enriched rats drank less morphine whether pre-exposed, naive or raised in either housing, without the body's qualification that differences appeared only in specific conditions; Table 1 shows Rat Park rats consuming more morphine than isolated rats during forced access (18.6 vs 13.3 mg per rat) and isolated rats drinking less on non-choice Nichols-cycle days.
reporting_issues.consequence: A claim that Rat Park rats consumed less morphine must state the conditions: choice days, sweetened low-concentration solutions, and housing at the time of testing.

reporting_issues.issue: Bozarth et al. is dated 1987 in the text but 1989 in the reference list (ref. 25), whose title covers heroin as well as cocaine; only a cocaine result is summarized.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the date and the heroin results should be checked in the original before it is cited.

reporting_issues.issue: Typographical slips in the accepted manuscript: 'Robbins' for Robins (PDF p. 1); 'LHCl' for MHCl in Table 1 (PDF p. 9); the 1981 F statistic is printed without degrees of freedom (PDF p. 9).
reporting_issues.consequence: None for the claims; the version of record may differ.

verification.source_read: Accepted manuscript PDF, 10 pages (text PDF pp. 1–5, references pp. 5–7, Table 1 pp. 8–10), all pages read on rendered pages and Table 1 checked at 150 dpi; pages differ from the version of record (Addiction 114(5):917–922, online 2018); no abstract heading in this version (the italic summary paragraph on PDF p. 1 serves as one); no supplement. Petrie 1996, the replication it summarizes, was read in the same session.
